name: Emeka Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I keep twelve thousand laying hens on Kestrel Farm, out past the end of Mill Lane. Free range, four sheds, and the birds go out onto the paddocks once it's light. I'm in the first shed by half five, walking the rows, listening, because a sick hen sounds different before she looks different. Then it's egg collection, grading, the packing centre lorry at eleven, and in the afternoon it's fences, foxes and feed orders.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the walk at dawn, honestly. You open the pop holes and the birds come out like kids let out of school. What wears me out is the paperwork from the packing centre and the bird flu rules, every time there's an outbreak somewhere you're shutting them in and disinfecting boots for three months.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been at it, and who else is on the farm?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Thirty-one years in eggs. I did my agriculture degree, worked for a big poultry company for six years and hated being a number, so Grace and I took the tenancy here. I've got two staff, Wendell, who's been with me nineteen years, and a young lad called Ifan who started in the spring. Grace teaches at the primary school, so the farm's mostly me and Wendell.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You said you keep records by hand. Tell me about that.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I write every shed's egg count in a pencil ledger my father bought me when I started. The packing centre wants it all on their app, and Ifan does that bit on his phone, but my numbers live in the book. I've never used one of these AI things and I don't see what I'd ask it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, that's how it should be. A tool is fine as long as somebody's in charge of it. At the farmers' meeting I'd probably say the packing centre will still find a way to squeeze us, AI or no AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it changes nothing for me. My problem has never been technology, it's that four supermarkets decide what an egg is worth. If AI stays a fancy search engine, I'll carry on not using it and nobody will be worse off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing new, really. I'd renew the paddock fencing on shed three, about four thousand in materials, which I'd planned anyway. Ifan might show me something on his phone and I'd nod and go back to the ledger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit smug, if I'm honest, because people kept telling me I was being left behind and here I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the supermarkets. What would you actually say about them at that meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say, that the price of a dozen eggs in the shop went up and our share went down. Last winter feed went up by a fifth and the packing centre gave us two pence a dozen extra. Wendell says I sound like a broken record, and he's right, but the record isn't wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Ifan ever push you to try these tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He tried once. He asked his phone why hens stop laying in November and read me the answer, and it was all things I'd told him the week before. I said, there you go, you've got two of us now, and one of them doesn't need charging.

S0.say: I'd say a tool is fine as long as someone's in charge of it. The real fight is still with the packing centre and the supermarkets, AI or not.
S0.think: Privately I think it changes nothing for me at all. My problem has always been the supermarkets setting the egg price, not any lack of technology.
S0.do: Renews the paddock fencing on shed three for about four thousand, as already planned. Keeps the pencil ledger and leaves the packing centre app to Ifan.
S0.feel: Calm and a little smug that his old ways still work.
S0.quote: I said, there you go, you've got two of us now, and one of them doesn't need charging.
S0.fieldNote: He hears every question through his long fight with the supermarkets, so AI barely registers. The smugness is mild and good-humoured. Worth noting that he relies on Ifan's phone for the packing centre app while saying he never uses the technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Second picture. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say if companies stop taking on young people, that's a scandal, and the government should make them. It's the same story as farming, everyone wants the experienced worker and nobody wants to train one. I'd put that on the union's page, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, slow is survivable. I'll be retired before it reaches the shed, probably. The bit that gets me is Ifan, because if the packing centre and the feed mill stop hiring beginners, my farm might be the only place that would take a lad like him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit Ifan down and make sure he learns everything Wendell knows, the vaccinations, the lighting programme, reading a hen. I'd sign him up for the poultry stockman's certificate, the college does it for about six hundred, and I'd pay. And I'd keep him on even in a bad egg year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly for the young ones. It's like watching a gate swing shut while they're still walking up the lane.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said slow is survivable. What would you notice first on the farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the vet's office and the packing centre. The girl who rings me about collection times might be a machine voice. I'd hate that, but I'd survive it. The hens wouldn't notice anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd pay for Ifan's course. Is that money you've got spare?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not spare, no. We've got maybe three months of bills put by, and six hundred is six hundred. But Wendell trained me in half the things I know about hens, years ago, and nobody paid him for it. It's my turn.

S1.say: I'd say it's a scandal if companies stop taking on young people, and government should make them hire. Farming has the same problem with nobody training beginners.
S1.think: I think slow is survivable for me and I'll likely retire before it reaches the shed. What worries me is lads like Ifan who need someone to give them a first job.
S1.do: Signs Ifan up for the poultry stockman's certificate at the college and pays the six hundred himself. Has Wendell teach Ifan vaccinations, lighting and reading a hen, and keeps him on through a bad year.
S1.feel: Uneasy, mostly on behalf of the young.
S1.quote: It's like watching a gate swing shut while they're still walking up the lane.
S1.fieldNote: His worry goes straight to the youngest person on his farm, not himself. He links paying for Ifan's training to a debt he owes Wendell, which says a lot about how he sees work. He spends real money from a thin cushion to keep that chain going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third picture. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need unions and proper rules. Those office people were told to get a degree and they'd be safe, and now look. I'd be at the march, if there was one, and I'd say the companies making the machines should pay for the people they put out of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it hits me sideways. Grace's sister Comfort works in the council's housing office, and she'd go. And my son Daniel does claims at an insurance firm in the city, which sounds to me exactly like routine office work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ring Daniel the same week and ask him straight what his job actually is all day. I'd tell him the spare room is there if he needs it, and that there's always work collecting eggs, though he'd laugh at that. I'd hold off on the new egg grader, about eighteen thousand, so we've got money if family needs it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and angry underneath. Daniel did everything right and it might not count for anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually say to Daniel on that phone call?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, son, what do you do from nine to five, really. And he'd say, Dad, it's complicated, and I'd say, then explain it slowly to your old man. If he can't explain it, maybe a machine can't do it either. If he can, that's when I'd worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're holding off on the grader. What does that cost you on the farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The old grader cracks more eggs, maybe two percent instead of one. That's real money over a year, a few thousand. But a cracked egg is cheaper than my son with no wages and a flat in the city.

S2.say: I'd say this is why we need unions and proper rules, and the companies making the machines should pay for the people they put out of work. I'd join any march going.
S2.think: Privately it hits me through family, not the farm. My son Daniel does insurance claims and Grace's sister works in the council housing office, and both sound like routine office work.
S2.do: Rings his son Daniel that week to ask what his job really involves and offers him the spare room. Postpones the eighteen-thousand new egg grader to keep money free for family.
S2.feel: Anxious and angry that his son did everything right and it may not count.
S2.quote: A cracked egg is cheaper than my son with no wages and a flat in the city.
S2.fieldNote: The threat lands on his son and sister-in-law, and his plans bend around them. He treats the farm as the family's safety net. His public anger is aimed at companies, while privately the feeling is closer to fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Fourth picture. Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the gains should go to everyone, full stop. If the machines are making a fortune, tax it and pay for the nurses, the teachers, the people thrown out. I'd say that loud, at the pub and online, and I wouldn't care who it annoyed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it scares me more for the town than for the shed. Mill Lane will fill up with city people who sold their flats for a fortune, buying old farmhouses, and they'll complain about the smell of my hens. Meanwhile half our customers at the farm gate will have no wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd talk to the landlord about the tenancy, because if land prices go mad he might sell to someone rich and I'd be out. I'd ask for a ten-year renewal in writing. I'd also join the tenants' association properly, which I've meant to do for years, and I'd go to the meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, I think. Not about the hens, but about losing the ground under them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said physical jobs are mostly untouched here. Doesn't that help you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On paper, yes. My hands are safe. But I don't own the farm, I rent it, and when house prices boom, tenants get pushed out. I've seen it happen to Wyn Probert two valleys over, the landlord sold to a man who wanted a view.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Grace say about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grace would say, Emeka, you've got the same fight every time, it's just a new name for it. She'd be right. She'd also say she's not moving at fifty-six, so I'd better win this one.

S3.say: I'd say the gains should go to everyone and the machines' profits should be taxed to pay for nurses, teachers and the people thrown out of work.
S3.think: Privately I'm more scared for the town and my tenancy than for the hens. City money would push up land prices and my landlord might sell to someone rich.
S3.do: Asks the landlord for a ten-year tenancy renewal in writing. Joins the tenants' association properly and starts going to meetings.
S3.feel: Alarmed, not about the work but about losing the land under it.
S3.quote: I've seen it happen to Wyn Probert two valleys over, the landlord sold to a man who wanted a view.
S3.fieldNote: He is the only person I've heard spot the danger in rising land prices for a tenant farmer. His job is safe but his home is not, and he sees that clearly. Grace's line about the same fight with a new name tells you how long he's been fighting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the end of the working countryside unless we fight it. I'd want the union, the tenants, everyone in one room. I'd say the robots should be owned by the people who work alongside them, or taxed so hard nobody can afford to replace a man with one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, poultry would be first. They've already got machines that roll down the shed and pick up floor eggs, and the big units would buy hundreds. My eggs would have to compete with eggs from a shed where nobody's paid a wage, and I'd lose. Wendell would lose his job before I lose mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't buy one, I'd say that now. I'd go to the packing centre and ask whether they'll pay a premium for eggs collected by people, like the free range premium. I'd talk to Wendell about his pension, because he's sixty-one, and see if I can get him to the finish line. And I'd probably start thinking about retiring two years early instead of fighting a war I can't win.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, and sad. Not panicked, because I'm nearly at the end anyway, but sad for the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd never buy one. What if every neighbour has one and you can't keep up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'll stop. I won't be the man who sacks Wendell after nineteen years to buy a robot on finance. I know that's stubborn. Grace says stubborn is my best quality and my worst one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep that pencil ledger. What happens to it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep it to the last day. When I hand back the keys I'll give it to Ifan. My count for the hens on the day the robots come, written in pencil, so somebody remembers there was a person doing it.

S4.say: I'd say this is the end of the working countryside unless we fight it. Robots should be owned by the workers alongside them, or taxed so hard nobody replaces a person with one.
S4.think: I think poultry would be first, because egg-collecting robots already exist and big units would buy hundreds. My eggs would lose on price, and Wendell would lose his job before I lose mine.
S4.do: Refuses to buy a robot and asks the packing centre about a premium for eggs collected by people. Works out how to get Wendell, aged sixty-one, to his pension, and considers retiring two years early.
S4.feel: Alarmed and sad for the job, but not panicked because he's near the end.
S4.quote: I won't be the man who sacks Wendell after nineteen years to buy a robot on finance.
S4.fieldNote: His refusal is about loyalty to Wendell more than fear of technology. He is the first in this group to talk about retiring early as a way out. The plan to hand Ifan the ledger is both a protest and a goodbye.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The last one, the robots, because it's the one where Wendell and Ifan both lose and I can't do anything about it. What would help is rules, real ones, that say a farm can't cut its workers just to buy a machine, and a fair price for eggs so I can afford to keep people. And a decent pension for farm workers, which we've never had.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the hens. Everyone talks about jobs, but a person walking a shed notices a hen that's off her feed a day before any machine would. I'm not saying I'm better than a robot. I'm saying I'm paying attention, and that counts for something.

headlineQuote: I won't be the man who sacks Wendell after nineteen years to buy a robot on finance.
portrait: Emeka Nakamura is fifty-eight and has kept free range laying hens for thirty-one years on a rented farm off Mill Lane, still counting eggs in a pencil ledger his father bought him. He sees every scenario through his long fight with supermarkets and egg prices, and through loyalty to his worker Wendell and young Ifan. The slower pictures barely touch him, but the faster ones hit his son's office job and threaten his tenancy as land prices rise. When robots arrive, he refuses to buy one and talks of retiring early rather than sacking Wendell.
biggestWorry: The robot picture worries him most, because both his workers would lose their jobs and his eggs couldn't compete on price.
whatWouldHelp: Real rules stopping farms cutting workers just to buy machines, a fair egg price so he can afford staff, and a decent pension for farm workers.
